questions.q: Why does the pipeline run the type check and lint before the integration tests?
questions.explain: Put cheap, likely failures first. There is no point spending minutes on a database and migrations for a change that does not compile.
options: Integration tests need the linter's output
They are fast and catch common mistakes, so a broken change fails in seconds instead of after starting a database
Linting changes the code the tests run

questions.q: How does a CI system decide that a step such as npm run lint failed?
questions.explain: Exit code 0 means success; anything else is failure. Every tool in the pipeline follows that contract, which is why a script that swallows errors (or prints them and exits 0) breaks the pipeline silently.
options: It searches the output for the word "error"
The command exits with a non-zero exit code
The step takes longer than a minute
It compares the output with the previous run

questions.q: In the generated project, a test passes { title: "…" } where the type requires { name: string }, yet npm run typecheck and npm test both pass. Why?
questions.explain: Nothing type-checks the test files. A second configuration that includes tests/, run as typecheck:tests, closes that gap.
options: TypeScript allows extra properties in tests
tsconfig.json only includes src/, and Vitest strips types without checking them
Vitest runs a different TypeScript version

questions.q: Which of these would a linter such as Biome report, while tsc with the generated settings accepts it?
questions.explain: The other three are type errors. A loose == and an unused variable are valid TypeScript but likely mistakes; that is the linter's job.
options: Calling a function with the wrong number of arguments
Importing a file that does not exist
Assigning a string to a number variable

questions.q: Why is npx biome lint risky in a project that has not installed @biomejs/biome?
questions.explain: npx resolves a bare name on the registry when it is not installed locally. Install tools as dev dependencies so the lockfile decides exactly which code runs.
options: npx downloads and runs whatever package is named biome on npm, which is a different package

questions.q: Why does the pipeline use npm ci rather than npm install?
questions.explain: CI must be reproducible: the same commit installs the same versions every time. npm install may resolve newer versions and rewrite the lockfile.
options: It installs exactly what package-lock.json lists, from a clean node_modules, and fails if the lockfile and package.json disagree
It updates every dependency to the latest version
It does not run install scripts

questions.q: The integration tests pass on a developer's laptop and fail on a clean clone with PAYMENTS_URL is not set. What is the real problem?
questions.explain: A clean clone has none of your local state. That is exactly why CI starts from nothing: it finds settings, files and packages that only exist on one machine.
options: The setting existed only in one developer's .env; it was never added to .env.example or to the CI and server environments

questions.q: The integration test file uses describe.skipIf(!process.env.DATABASE_URL). What is the trade-off?
questions.explain: Skipping is convenient locally and dangerous in CI. Check the test counts in the CI log, or make the CI job fail when the variable is missing.
options: The tests become faster in CI
Running it without a database is not an error, but if CI forgot to set DATABASE_URL the tests would silently skip, so CI must always set it
Vitest cannot skip a whole file

questions.q: npm audit reports high-severity advisories in mysql2 and deepmerge-ts, pulled in by the Prisma CLI, and suggests npm audit fix --force, which downgrades Prisma a major version. What is the best first move?
questions.explain: Triage: is it reachable, how bad, what is the cheapest safe fix? Patched versions existed, so overrides removed the findings without a breaking downgrade. A documented, expiring exception is the fallback.
options: Check whether patched versions exist and force them with overrides, then run the full pipeline; accept a finding only with a reason and an expiry date
Ignore it, because the app does not use MySQL

questions.q: gitleaks finds a GitHub token committed three weeks ago. What must happen first?
questions.explain: Once pushed, a secret must be treated as known. Rotating it makes the leaked copy useless; cleaning the history comes after, if at all.
options: Delete the file in a new commit
Rewrite the Git history to remove the commit
Revoke the token and issue a new one, because anyone who fetched the repository may have it

questions.q: What does permissions: contents: read at the top of the workflow achieve?
questions.explain: Least privilege: if a step or a dependency is compromised, the token it can steal cannot push code or publish packages. Only the build job adds packages: write.
options: It hides the repository from other users
The automatic GITHUB_TOKEN of every job can only read the repository unless a job asks for more

questions.q: The deploy jobs use concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }. What happens when two merges reach production deploy at the same time?
questions.explain: Cancelling a deploy halfway could leave a migration applied without its app. Queueing keeps each deploy whole.
options: The newer one cancels the older one halfway through
They run one after the other, so two deploys never interleave on one environment

questions.q: actionlint warns about run: echo "deploying ${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}". Why?
questions.explain: That is script injection. Put the value in env: and use "$MESSAGE": the shell then treats it as data.
options: Commit messages can be too long for echo
The expression is pasted into the script before the shell runs it, so a crafted message becomes shell code
echo is not available on the runner

questions.q: A pull request from a fork runs your workflow. Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Code from a fork is untrusted. The checks still run, but nothing that needs secrets or deploys does.
options: It gets all repository secrets, like any other run
GitHub does not pass repository or environment secrets to it, and the deploy jobs do not run because they require a push to main
It can push images to your registry
It runs on your production server

questions.q: Both deploy jobs refer to secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY. How do they get different keys?
questions.explain: Environment secrets override repository secrets of the same name for jobs in that environment, and production can require an approval before its secrets are ever used.
options: By using different secret names in each job
Each job runs in a different environment (staging or production), and each environment has its own value for the secret
The key is chosen by the branch name

questions.q: Which secret should the CI system not hold in this design?
questions.explain: Application secrets live in a file on each server, readable only by the deploy user. CI only needs to reach the server and name the release, so a compromised CI leaks less.
options: The SSH key to reach the server
The database password and the payment provider settings
None: CI should hold every secret

questions.q: GitHub masks secret values in logs. Which line still leaks?
questions.explain: Masking replaces the exact value. An encoding or a part of the secret is a different string and is printed in full.

questions.q: Why does the pipeline build a separate migrate image from the same Dockerfile?
questions.explain: The generated runtime stage keeps only production dependencies. A stage built from the same commit carries the CLI and the migration files, and runs only when asked.
options: Because migrations must run as root
The production image drops dev dependencies, including the Prisma CLI, so it cannot run prisma migrate deploy
Because migrations need a different Node.js version
To make the app image slower to build

questions.q: What would happen without set -euo pipefail at the top of deploy.sh if the migration step failed?
questions.explain: By default bash ignores failing commands and runs the next line. -e stops at the first failure, -u treats unset variables as errors, and pipefail makes a failure inside a pipe count.
options: The script would carry on and start the new app against an unmigrated database

questions.q: A release added a column with a default. The next release is bad and you start the previous image again. What happens to the database?
questions.explain: Code rolls back, the database only moves forward. That is safe as long as every migration keeps the previous release working: add, don't rename or drop, until you are sure.
options: The old image refuses to start
Nothing: the column stays, and the old code works because it never mentions it
The data in the column is deleted
The old image applies its own migrations again, dropping the column

questions.q: A migration that already ran in production has a wrong default. What should you do?
questions.explain: Applied migrations are history. Prisma stores a checksum and refuses a changed file, and an edited file would make new databases differ from production.
options: Edit the migration file, since it is only SQL
Delete it and generate it again
Add a new migration that changes the default
Change the default by hand in production

questions.q: Why should the deploy wait for /health (a readiness check that includes the database) rather than for "the container started"?
questions.explain: The bad release in the lesson started a container that crashed on a missing PAYMENTS_URL. Only a check of what users need caught it and triggered the rollback.
options: A process can start and still be unable to serve, for example because a required setting is missing or the database is unreachable

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After the first failure every later stage is skipped, and deploy is the last stage, so nothing reaches users.
options:
pass install
pass type check
FAIL unit tests
skip build
skip deploy
deployed: no

pass install
pass type check
FAIL unit tests
pass build
pass deploy
deployed: yes

pass install
pass type check
FAIL unit tests
deployed: no

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Jobs whose needs are all done run together. verify and security need nothing, so they run in parallel; build waits for both branches.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "tests" is not a job name; the job is test. actionlint reports the same thing as [job-needs] before you push.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Masking matches the exact string. Upper-casing, splitting or encoding a secret produces something the mask does not recognise, so never print derived values.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Registry names must be lower case. Every build gets the commit tag; a version tag is added only for a Git tag, as an extra name for the same image.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The commented-out line starts with #, so it does not count as documenting the setting. A check like this fails the build before a clean environment fails to start.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The low finding is below the gate. mysql2 has a valid exception; the one for deepmerge-ts expired, so it fails. Dates in YYYY-MM-DD form compare correctly as strings.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Looking back from d4: c3 was never healthy, b2 works with schema 2. With schema 3 live, no earlier release fits. From c3, the nearest earlier healthy release is b2, which also handles schema 1.

questions.q: Prisma names migrations with a timestamp prefix. What does this print?
questions.explain: Applied migrations are skipped; the rest run in name order, which the timestamp prefix makes chronological. That is why the same command is safe to run on every deploy.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first wait uses up three answers (no answer, 503, 503) and gives up. The second call starts where the probe left off and gets 200 at once. A limit on attempts is what turns "never healthy" into a rollback instead of a stuck deploy.
options:
not healthy: roll back
healthy after 1

not healthy: roll back
not healthy: roll back

questions.q: Write runStages(stages). Each stage is { name, run } where run() returns an exit code. Run them in order, stop at the first non-zero code, and return { passed, failed, skipped }: the names that passed, the name that failed (or null), and the names never run.
questions.explain: The last line proves the skipped stages never ran: stopping early is not just a report, it prevents the side effects of later stages, deploy above all.

questions.q: Write missingSettings(envText, required): parse lines of the form NAME=value (ignore comments and blank lines) and return the required names that are missing or have an empty value.
questions.explain: An empty value is as bad as a missing one, and a commented-out line is missing. Running such a check before a deploy turns a failed release and a rollback into a clear message that nothing was changed.

questions.q: Write auditGate(vulnerabilities, exceptions, today). vulnerabilities maps package names to { severity }. Return the sorted names with severity high or critical that have no exception whose expires date (YYYY-MM-DD) is today or later.
questions.explain: An exception still counts on its expiry day and fails the day after. Sorting makes the gate's output stable, so two runs on the same report print the same list.

questions.q: Write breaksPreviousRelease(sql, columnsUsedByPrevious) for simple migrations. Return true if the SQL renames or drops a column the previous release uses, or adds a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT. Match case-insensitively.
questions.explain: Dropping a column the previous release no longer uses is the "contract" step and is safe. A text check like this is a quick warning; the reliable test is running the previous release's queries against the migrated schema, as the lesson does with PGlite.

questions.q: Write maskLog(lines, secrets) that replaces every occurrence of each secret with ***, but first registers, for every secret, its base64 form (btoa) as a secret too, so the encoded value is hidden as well.
questions.explain: GitHub lets a step register extra values to mask (the ::add-mask:: command) for exactly this reason. It still cannot guess every transformation, so the rule stays: never print secrets or anything derived from them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: build needs test, which needs deploy, which needs build: a cycle, so none of them can ever start. GitHub rejects such a workflow, and actionlint reports it before you push.

questions.q: A tiny checksum stands in for Prisma's SHA-256 of each applied migration. What does this print?
questions.explain: Changing one word of an applied migration changes its checksum, so the tool can refuse to continue instead of letting new databases and production drift apart. New files are simply pending.

questions.q: Write rollbackTarget(history, current, liveSchema). history is in deploy order, each { tag, worksWithSchemaUpTo, healthy }. Return the tag of the most recent release before current that was healthy and works with liveSchema, or "fix forward" if there is none.
questions.explain: From ddc4ac4 with schema 2 live, the only earlier release handles schema 1 at most, so rolling back would break it. Knowing that before an incident is what the schema bookkeeping is for.
